The server implements the MCP streamable HTTP transport on a single path, /mcp.
Route
Behavior
POST /mcp
JSON-RPC requests, notifications, responses to server requests, and batches of those. A request answers 200 with the JSON-RPC response; a notification or a response answers 202 with an empty body.
GET /mcp
opens the text/event-stream channel of the session. A comment (: ping) is sent immediately so the client knows the stream is live, then one event: message per server message.
DELETE /mcp
terminates the session: 204 when it was live, 404 when it was already gone, 400 without the session header.
Header
Mcp-Session-Id
returned by initialize, the client sends it back on every subsequent request. An unknown or expired value answers 404, which is the signal for the client to initialize agai

This page is for contributors, and for anyone wanting to know what happens between an HTTP request and a tool call.
MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0. Fusion already generates a complete JSON-RPC stack at build time, so the implementation is mostly wiring rather than protocol code:
the MCP methods are plain @JsonRpc methods (MCPJSONRPCProtocol) registered in the same registry as the application ones,
tools/call re-enters JsonRpcHandler, so a tool invocation follows the exact same code path as a direct JSON-RPC call - binding, validation, error mapping included,
the descriptors come from the OpenRPC document the annotation processor writes in META-INF/fusion/jsonrpc/openrpc.json,
only the transport is specific: sessions, SSE, headers, and the routing of client responses.

MCPClient is shipped in the main artifact - it has no test framework dependency - and drives a server the way a real client does: it runs the handshake, keeps the Mcp-Session-Id header across calls and reads the SSE channel.
Every call returns a CompletionStage, which is what a MCP interaction needs: a tool using sampling or elicitation only answers once the client responded on the SSE channel, so its invocation cannot be awaited first.

A prompt is a template the user picks - a slash command in an IDE, an entry in a menu - and not something the model calls on its own. Flag a JSON-RPC method with @MCPPrompt:
Two constraints, both coming from the specification:
the method must return a PromptResponse - or a CompletionStage<PromptResponse>,
prompt arguments are always strings, so only declare String parameters.
prompts/list exposes the name, the description and the arguments - name, description and whether it is required - all derived from the signature exactly like for a tool. prompts/get invokes the method and returns the expanded messages.

A resource is data the client can read and attach to a conversation: a file, a configuration, a database row, an API payload. Resources are dynamic by nature - they are data, not code - so unlike tools and prompts they are not mapped on JSON-RPC methods but provided at runtime by any bean implementing MCPResources:
All the implementations are used and visited in bean priority order (@Order), which is how a module can add its own resources without knowing the others. The resources capability - and the related methods - is only advertised when at least one implementation exists.

Roots
MCP is bidirectional: the server can talk to the client too. Everything it sends goes through the SSE channel the client opens with GET /mcp, and comes in two flavours:
notifications, one way: logging, list_changed, progress,
requests, awaiting an answer: sampling, elicitation, roots. The client posts its response back on POST /mcp.
messages are buffered per session, so nothing is lost when no stream is currently open - a client reconnecting gets what it missed. But a client which never opens a stream never receives anything, and a request sent to it times out (fusion.mcp.clientRequestTimeout, 30s by default).
